title: Enterovirus D68 in Europe, 2025: continent-wide predominance of subclade A2/D and shift from pediatric to adult cases

analysis.research_question_and_background: Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) has predominantly caused infections in children, and detected cases have mainly been infected by subclade B3. This study aimed to detail the molecular epidemiology of the 2025 season in Europe.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Case and sequencing data was collected from members in the European Non-Polio Enterovirus Network (ENPEN). The participating sites included both clinical and public health laboratories.
analysis.methods: Data was collected from 13 countries at 23 sites. The detection of interclade recombinant variants highlights a need to supplement regular VP1-based genotyping with whole-genome sequencing.
analysis.main_results: There were 187 clinical cases infected with EV-D68 and 127 detections in wastewater. Age data were available for 76% (143/187), among which 90 cases were adults. VP1-based genotyping showed subclade A2/D to predominate in all age groups and across all participating countries, as well as in the sewage sampling performed at one site.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The observed shift towards adult cases and subclade A2/D predominance warrants continued monitoring to determine whether this represents a sustained epidemiological change.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings highlight the importance of continued surveillance to understand potential changes in the epidemiology of EV-D68 and to inform public health strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the reliance on data from 13 countries at 23 sites, which may affect generalisability. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigates the molecular epidemiology of Enterovirus D68 (EV-D68) in Europe during 2025, noting a shift from predominantly pediatric cases to adult cases. The research aimed to detail this change, utilizing data from the European Non-Polio Enterovirus Network (ENPEN) across 13 countries and 23 sites. VP1-based genotyping revealed that subclade A2/D became predominant in all age groups and countries, with 90 adult cases identified from 143 with age data. Two interclade recombinant sequences were detected among 22 whole genome sequences, underscoring the need for whole-genome sequencing in addition to VP1-based genotyping. The authors suggest that this shift may indicate a sustained epidemiological change, emphasizing the importance of continued monitoring. The study's findings have implications for public health strategies, particularly in tracking and understanding the evolving patterns of EV-D68 infections. However, the study's observational design and limited geographic scope may affect the generalisability of its results, resulting in moderate confidence in the evidence.

analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results provide insights into the molecular mechanisms of EV-A71 replication and antiviral signaling, which could inform future research on therapeutic strategies targeting DDX58 or related pathways.

title: Hand, Foot, and Mouth Disease with Probable Intrafamilial Transmission in a 15-Month-Old Infant: A Case Report

analysis.research_question_and_background: Hand, foot, and mouth disease (HFMD) is an acute exanthema disease caused by a viral infection which is generally self-limiting, most often caused by Coxsackievirus A16 and Enterovirus 71, and more often attacks children under five years of age.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Problem: Transmission within the family through direct contact with secretions or lesion fluid from infected individuals is a recognized transmission route, however case reports that specifically state the possibility of intrafamilial transmission in children under two years old are still rare in the literature.
analysis.methods: Case report: We report a case of HFMD in a 15 month old boy who was brought to the outpatient facility with complaints of reddish rashes around the mouth, hands and feet since two days previously, preceded by fever as a prodromal symptom.
analysis.main_results: Physical examination showed maculopapular and vesicular lesions in the perioral region, right wrist, and bilateral lower extremities, with generalized distribution and miliary to lenticular size.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: A history of close contact with an older sibling who experienced similar symptoms approximately one week previously supports the possibility of intrafamilial transmission between siblings.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Management: The diagnosis is made clinically without laboratory supporting examinations.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: This case emphasizes the importance of a systematic history of intrafamilial contact history in children with suspected HFMD, as well as the need for targeted family education to break the chain of transmission in the household environment.

The diagnosis was made clinically without laboratory confirmation, and the patient received supportive treatment including paracetamol syrup, mupirocin ointment, and immunostimulants. The report underscores the importance of documenting family contact history in HFMD cases and implementing targeted education to prevent transmission within households. While the study provides insight into intrafamilial transmission patterns, it is limited by its case report design and lack of laboratory evidence, which reduces the strength of the findings.
